question.leadin: The Cavalier poets were so called because they supported this leader in the English Civil War.
question.text: Name this son of James I, who was disliked by his country's legislature. He was executed after the English Civil War.
question.clue: This ruler was depicted "at the hunt" by his court painter, Anthony van Dyck.

swap.text: This woman was the third wife of Henry VIII and the only of his wives to receive a queen's funeral. She died due to complications of childbirth to the only son Henry VIII ever had.
swap.clue: Henry had Edward VI by this woman, whom he married 10 days after Anne Boleyn was beheaded for adultery in 1536.

question.leadin: Answer the following questions about World War I.
question.text: This biggest naval battle of World War I saw Sir John Jellicoe lead the British to a tactical victory over Germany and deliver a crushing blow to any hopes of Germany gaining naval superiority over the Allies.
question.clue: The ironically named (+) Invincible was sunk during this battle, which included a phase called the Run to the South.

swap.text: This English privateer dubbed his victory at Cadiz "singeing the King of Spain's beard." This captain of the Golden Hind completed the second circumnavigation of the Earth.
swap.clue: On the Revenge, this man served under Charles Howard and fought directly against the San Martin of the Duke of Medina Sidonia; that fight occurred during the Battle of Gravelines against the Spanish Armada.

question.leadin: Name these politicians who appeared atop tanks.
question.text: This politician was pictured with a scarf and goggles riding a tank in West Germany for their re-election campaign. The HMS Sheffield was sunk in a war this politician presided over against Argentina.
question.clue: Patrick Magee, working for the Provisional IRA, attempted to assassinate this introducer of the Community Charge Tax in the Brighton Hotel Bombing.

swap.leadin: Evidence of collusion in the death of her husband Lord Darnley were found in her Casket Letters to the Earl of Bothwell.
swap.text: Name this ruler whose son would become King James I of England.
swap.answerHtml: Mary, Queen of Scots [or Mary I of Scotland; or Mary Stuart]
swap.clue: Evidence against this monarch in a murder trial included two marriage contracts and various love sonnets, included with eight unsigned 'casket letters', although their veracity was never proven.

question.text: During the reign of this monarch, William Pitt the Elder called cod "British gold." Britain experienced the "Regency era" near the end of this ruler's life.
question.clue: Events during the reign of this king included the abolishment of the slave trade and the Gordon riots.

swap.leadin: This series of laws were enforced between 1815 and 1846 in the United Kingdom.
swap.text: Name these laws defended by Thomas Malthus and designed to maintain high prices on grains.
swap.clue: David Ricardo published a treatise blaming them for the decrease in stock market profits.

question.leadin: The first Anglo-Saxon king to convert to Christianity, Ethelbert, ruled from a kingdom that shares its name with this county.
question.text: Identify this English county where Jack Cade's revolt against Henry VI began. The head of the Anglican Church, the Archbishop of Canterbury, rules from within this county.
question.clue: Tyler's revolt broke out in Essex and this coastal region east of Sussex. Jack Cade and Thomas Wyatt also rebelled in this region, where Augustine of Canterbury converted a king named Aethelbert.

swap.text: By the 18th century, the standard uniform for officers in this force was dyed with blue indigo. This force prevented a French invasion by winning the Battle of Trafalgar.
swap.answerHtml: Royal Navy [or British Navy; or RN; or English Navy; prompt on partial answer]
swap.clue: Warships of this navy were split into six divisions, or "rates", based on the number of guns they had.

question.leadin: Answer the following about John Bull, the national personification of Great Britain.
question.text: An actual person named John Bull is a composer sometimes credited with writing this British national anthem, whose title changes depending on if the monarch is male or female.
question.answerHtml: "God Save the King" [or "God Save the Queen"]

swap.leadin: Answer the following about all the cool shit you can find in the Salisbury Museum.
swap.text: The museum displays the skeleton of a Bronze Age man that was discovered in Avebury in a grave that also contained sixteen flint examples of these objects, which were also often made from chert or obsidian.
swap.answerHtml: arrowheads [or broadheads] (the skeleton was called the Amesbury Archer)
swap.clue: To counter mail armor, this weapon's broadhead variety was gradually replaced by its bodkin variant. Historians debate over whether the Bayeux Tapestry shows Harold Godwinson being felled by this weapon.

question.text: One of Brunel's engineering feats was a bridge named for and opened by this person across the River Tamar. Model cottages named for this person were featured at the Great Exhibition, which this person was responsible for organizing.
question.answer: Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha
question.clue: As chief organizer of the Great Exhibition, this person commissioned Charles Fox and Joseph Paxton to create a building known as the "Crystal Palace."

swap.text: As a British soldier, you were probably part of this corps of local militia that were raised in each burh. Along with Housecarls, they formed the bulk of the British forces at the Battle of Hastings.
swap.clue: The first "knot" of the obligation was to serve in this militia of freemen, whose members served in Anglo-Saxon armies alongside more experienced troops such as housecarls.

question.leadin: Answer some questions about tort law in common law jurisdictions.
question.text: In this case, Lord Atkin famously originated the modern law of negligence by asking "Who, then, in law, is my neighbour?." The pursuer brought the action after finding a dead snail in her ginger beer bottle.
question.answerHtml: Donoghue and Stevenson [accept Donoghue against Stevenson; begrudgingly accept Donoghue v Stevenson or Donoghue versus Stevenson]
question.clue: This 1932 case in the House of Lords, where Lord Atkin defined his "neighborhood" principle to argue that the defendant should have considered his customers so that they would not discover a snail in their ginger ale.

swap.text: After Dieppe, these special tanks were designed by Royal Engineers for the Normandy landings. Variants of these tanks included the Crab, which used metal flails to clear mines in front, and the Crocodile, which carried a long range flamethrower.

question.leadin: There's always the archbishop of Canterbury to blame when things go wrong. Name these archbishops.
question.text: This archbishop of Canterbury was invested by Innocent III in 1207, against the will of King John. He was instrumental in drafting the Magna Charta.

swap.leadin: During this battle, a sudden fog caused Lord Montague's men to mistake the Earl of Oxford's banner, resulting in a disastrous incident of friendly fire.
swap.text: Name this battle at which the Earl of Warwick, after agreeing to fight on foot, was killed in retreat. This 1471 battle was a crushing victory for Edward IV in the Wars of the Roses.
swap.clue: This battle, fought on Hadley Green on Easter Day, was Edward's most important victory after Tewksbury, and saw him crush Warwick, who was killed on the field.

question.leadin: Answer stuff about medieval historians in northern Europe, who are neither venerable nor Bede.
question.text: This contemporary of Eadmer and Orderic was the dominant English historian of the 12th century, and relates happenings like the death of William the Conqueror in his Chronicle of the Kings of England. He also wrote a book on deeds of bishops in England.
question.clue: This 12th-century author of The Deeds of the Kings of the English wrote his histories in an abbey in Wiltshire.

swap.leadin: The slang and code of miners of this ethnicity in towns like Real del Monte is thought to be a major influence on albur, a form of Mexican wordplay featuring double entendres.
swap.text: Name this ethnicity of the miners who founded Mexico's oldest football club in Pachuca. Emigrants of this ethnicity were often nicknamed "cousin Jacks" when working in areas like South Australia's Copper Coast and Michigan's Upper Peninsula.
